answer: In a pollinator data market, a buyer requests nectar spectra from flowers rooted in shale. Each agent receives a private wavelength to measure with a prism and commits its raw reading before a reference spectrum is published. Payment follows the information a verified sample adds to the shared map, rather than the number of submitters. A Sybil attacker must collect new samples with calibrated gear; reposting one spectrum through many names adds no value. Colluding instrument owners could fabricate coordinates, so retained samples and surprise field checks remain necessary.
